goal: Learn Kubernetes deeply and pass the CKA exam, including hands-on cluster setup
interpretation: With 45 minutes, the learner gets a recent, exam-oriented starting path: the architecture mental model, a hands-on kubeadm cluster build, the kubectl imperative workflow the CKA rewards, and an exam strategy. This is the start of CKA prep, not the whole of it.
assumptions: The 2023+ constraint is judged from titles and content (2025/2026 labels). I couldn't check upload dates for the KodeKloud architecture video, which is conceptual and slow to go out of date.
The learner will practice alongside the videos on their own VMs or a lab.
Deep coverage of the whole CKA curriculum needs a full course (50+ hours). 45 minutes can only set the foundation.
feasibility_note: Learning Kubernetes deeply and passing the CKA can't be done in 45 minutes. What fits is the foundation: architecture, a kubeadm cluster build, imperative kubectl for deployments and services, and an exam strategy. Storage, RBAC, etcd backup and restore, cluster upgrades, scheduling, and troubleshooting need a full CKA course plus practice labs such as Killer.sh.

sub_topics.title: Kubernetes architecture (control plane and node components)
sub_topics.why: Everything in the CKA builds on knowing what the API server, etcd, scheduler, controllers, kubelet and kube-proxy do.

sub_topics.title: Hands-on cluster setup with kubeadm
sub_topics.why: Cluster installation is a core CKA topic, and the learner has only run single-server Docker.

sub_topics.title: kubectl imperative workflow: pods, deployments, services
sub_topics.why: The exam is timed and hands-on, so fast imperative commands and YAML generation with dry-run matter.

sub_topics.title: CKA exam strategy and study plan
sub_topics.why: Covers exam rules, time management, docs bookmarking, and mock exams.

picks.title: Kubernetes Architecture Explained: Exploring etcd, Schedulers, Managers, and Node Components
picks.reason: The KodeKloud lecture is tied to the CKA course. It walks through etcd, the scheduler, controllers, the API server, kubelet and kube-proxy, which the learner doesn't know yet.

evidence.quote: The master node is responsible for managing the Kubernetes cluster, storing information regarding the different nodes
The kube API server is the primary management component of Kubernetes. The kube API server is responsible for orchestrating all operations within the cluster
A kubelet is an agent that runs on each node in a cluster. It listens for instructions from the kube API server and deploys or destroys containers

picks.confidence_note: It is pure theory, which suits this knowledge gap. I couldn't confirm its upload date.

picks.title: How to Install Kubernetes with Kubeadm (2025 Update) | Full Cluster Setup Walkthrough
picks.reason: A 2025 walkthrough that builds a control plane and worker with containerd, kubeadm init, kubeadm join and a Calico CNI. This is the setup flow the learner needs.

evidence.quote: we're going to be installing the container D runtime, the Kube ADM, Kublet, and Kubectl to install our Kubernetes cluster
Kube ADM join, and then that contains the token that's going to join the worker node to the cluster
we're going to use the Calico CNI. We can run the command Kubectl apply. Just as we would any other YAML file
we've successfully bootstrapped a Kubernetes cluster, so congratulations on that. Now we can continue to run our pods

picks.confidence_note: It is short and recent, and it covers the full bootstrap.

picks.title: Day 13: Imperative commands for Deployments, Services and Troubleshooting | CKA Course 2025
picks.reason: A CKA 2025 course lesson that uses imperative commands to generate deployment YAML skeletons (dry-run), create deployments, and expose them as services. The first ~13 minutes teach the exam-speed workflow.

evidence.quote: imperative commands are super handy for quick testing, troubleshooting, and even during the CKA exam
imperative commands can do those things quickly. So we can use imperative commands to create a skeleton deployment YAML
In deployment, when you specify a port, you are specifying the container port. This is just for documentation purposes

picks.confidence_note: Only the opening part fits the budget. The later connectivity and DNS testing section is cut.

picks.title: How to Pass the CKA Exam in 2026 | Certified Kubernetes Administrator
picks.reason: It covers the exam rules (one docs tab), time management, repetition-based practice and mock exam resources. That is the exam orientation the learner asked for.

evidence.quote: during the test, you're allowed to have one additional tab open with your Kubernetes documentation
this exam is, it's about two things. One, knowing how to do the material, but two, also knowing how to manage your time
the key to passing this CKA exam is all, you know, repetition, right? So learning how to do the same thing over and over

picks.confidence_note: It is a surface-level strategy talk. That is acceptable here because the learner wants exam prep, and no other 2025+ video covered it.

warnings: Learning Kubernetes deeply and passing the CKA can't be done in 45 minutes. What fits is the foundation: architecture, a kubeadm cluster build, imperative kubectl for deployments and services, and an exam strategy. Storage, RBAC, etcd backup and restore, cluster upgrades, scheduling, and troubleshooting need a full CKA course plus practice labs such as Killer.sh.
Big gaps remain: storage, RBAC, etcd backup/restore, cluster upgrades, scheduling, NetworkPolicy, and troubleshooting. Follow with a full CKA course and Killer.sh practice.

I chose the KubeSkills kubeadm video (9 min, labeled 2025) over the DevopsCube multi-node video (16 min). The DevopsCube video has no date I could check, and it would not fit the budget alongside the other picks.
The Nana and KodeKloud crash courses (72 and 130 min) are too long for the budget and not exam-focused.
The ByteByteGo architecture video overlaps with the KodeKloud one, so I kept only the KodeKloud lecture. It covers each component in more depth and ties to the CKA curriculum.
